Parent: "Sighed Mayzie, a lazy bird hatching an egg: 'I'm tired and I'm bored and I've kinks in my leg from sitting, just sitting here day after day. It's work! How I hate it! I'd much rather play. I will take a vacation, fly off for a rest, if I could find someone to stay on my nest. If I could find someone, I would fly away free.'"
Child: (continuing to sit on the parent's lap, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Then Horton the Elephant passed by her tree. 'Hello,' calls the lazy bird, smiling her best. 'You have nothing to do and I do need a rest. Would you like to sit on the egg in my nest?'"
Child: (closely watching the tablet, somewhat relaxed in the parent's embrace)

Parent: "That was helpful. The elephant laughed. Ha-ha-ha-ha! 'Why, of all silly things, I haven't feathers and I haven't wings. Me on your egg? Why, that doesn't make sense. Your egg is so small, madam, and so immense.'"
Child: (staying engaged, still looking at the tablet)

Parent: "'Tut-tut,' answers Mayzie, 'I know you are not small, but I'm sure you can do it, no trouble at all. Just sit on my egg softly. You are gentle and can. Come, be a good fellow, I know you won't mind.'"
Child: (looking at the tablet, engaged in the story)
Parent: "I can't," said the elephant. "Please," begged the bird. "I won't be gone long."
Child: (looking at the tablet, listening intently)
Child: (glancing up at the parent for a moment, then back at the tablet)

Child: (looking back at the tablet)

Parent: "Sir, I gave you my word. I will hurry right back. Why, I will never be missed." Just what happened?

Child: (listening attentively, eyes on the tablet)

Parent: "Very well," said the elephant. "Since you insist. You want a vacation. Go fly off and take it. I will sit on your egg and I will try not to break it. I'll stay and be faithful. I mean what I say."
Child: (nods slightly, still focused on the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet, sitting on parent's lap)
Parent: "Toodle-oo!" Sang out Mayzie and fluttered away.
Child: (continuing to look at the tablet, pointing at the screen)
Parent: (pointing at the screen) How could that have happened? Sit on egg.

Parent: Um-hmm, um-hmm. "Mm, the first thing to do," murmured Horton. "Let's see, the first thing to do is to prop up this tree. And make it much stronger, that has to be done, before I get on it. I must weigh a ton."

Parent: "Yes. Then carefully, tenderly, gently he crept up the trunk to the nest where the little egg slept. Ugh! Then Horton the Elephant said, 'Now, that's that.'"

Parent: "What did he do?"

Parent: "He lay on it."

Parent: "That's right. Yeah, he blew, too. Right? Before that, is there anything? No. Yeah, he put something here, right? I didn't know this. Yeah. Oh, what will he say? Broken. I see you have something."

Parent: "Then Horton the Elephant smiled, 'Now, that's that.' Oh, did I touch something? And he sat, and he sat, and he sat, and he sat. Even for that, I think it's very difficult. What do you think? Maybe it's not comfortable at all."
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: And he sat all that day and he kept the egg warm and he sat all that night through a terrible storm. It poured and it lightninged, there was thunder and it rumbled. "And this isn't much fun", the poor elephant grumbled. "I wish she'd come back, because I'm cold and I'm wet." Maybe he's also very hungry.

Child: (slightly turned towards the book)
Parent: You don't feel comfortable with that? Uh-huh? It's very hard.

Parent: "And having such fun and such a wonderful rest, she decided she'd never go back to her nest. Oh! She don't want to go back to her nest. So Horton kept sitting there, day after day, and soon it was autumn. Aw, do you think he eats anything? He sleep, maybe? Ah, it's very hard."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, thinking)

Parent: "The leaves blew away, and then came the winter, the snow and the sleet, and icicles hung from his trunk and his feet. But Horton kept sitting and said with a sneeze, 'I'll stay on this egg, and I won't let it freeze. I mean what I said, and I said what I meant, an elephant's faithful one hundred percent.'"
Child: (looks slightly puzzled, with a questioning look)
Parent: "One question, why the egg he didn't get up? Where? What's in it?"
Child: (looks back at the tablet, curious)

Parent: "So poor Horton sat there the whole winter through. And then came the springtime, with troubles anew. His friends gathered around and they shouted with glee, 'Look! Horton the Elephant is up in a tree!' They pointed, they teased him, they yawned, 'How absurd! Old Horton the Elephant is thinking he is a bird!' Is that funny?"
Child: (smiles, engaged by the story)
Child: (looking at the tablet, appears to be engaged)
Parent: "Mm-mm (negative)"
Child: (still looking at the tablet, seems curious)

Parent: "That is not funny at all. They laughed and they laughed and they all ran away. And Horton was lonely. He wanted to play, but he sat on the egg and continued to say, "I mean what I said and I said what I mean, and an elephant's faithful one hundred percent." But why he told the bird to get all the egg? I don't understand."
Child: (slightly leans forward, more engaged, slightly puzzled expression)

Parent: "No matter what happens, this egg must be tended. But poor Horton's trouble were far, far from ended, for while Horton sat there, so faithful, so kind, three hunters came sneaking up softly behind. He heard the men's footsteps, he turned with a start. Three rifles were aiming right straight at his heart."
Child: (sitting upright, looking at the tablet, seems focused on the story)

Parent: "What he should do? Uh-oh. Did he run? He did not. Horton stayed on that nest. He held his head high, and the threw out his chest and he looked at the hunters as much as to say, "Shoot if you must, but I won't run away. I mean what I said and I said what I meant, an elephant's faithful one hundred percent.""
Child: (points at the tablet, possibly pointing to an image or text, showing interest)
Child: (looking at the tablet, sitting next to the parent)
Parent: "But the men didn't shoot, much to Horton's surprise. They dropped their three guns and they stared with wide eyes. 'Look!' They all shouted."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: "'Can such a thing be? An elephant sitting on top of a tree.' Not a bird."
Child: (focused on the tablet)
Parent: "'It's strange, it's amazing, it's wonderful, new! Don't shoot him. We'll catch him. That's just what we will do."
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Let's take him alive. Why he's terribly funny. We'll sell him back home to a circus for money."
Child: (engaged and looking at the tablet)
Parent: "And the first thing he knew, he had built a big wagon,."
Child: (maintains focus on the tablet)
Parent: "with ropes on the front for the pullers to drag on. They dug up his tree. Ugh, actually [inaudible]. And they put it inside, with Horton so sad that he practically cried."
Child: (watching the tablet attentively)
Parent: "'We are off!' The men shouted, and off they all went, with Horton unhappy one hundred percent."
Child: (continues to pay attention to the tablet)
Parent: "Up out of the jungle, up in the sky, up over the mountains ten thousand feet high. Then down, down the mountains, down to the sea, went the cart with the elephant as well as the tree."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Where does he want to go?"
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Then out of the wagon, and on the ship, all over the ocean, and oh, what a trip. Floating, and tossing, and splash with a spray..."
Child: (still looking at the tablet)

Parent: "...and Horton sat day after day after day. 'I meant what I said and I said what I meant, but oh, am I seasick, one hundred percent!' After bobbing around for two weeks like a cork, they landed at last in the town of..."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "...New York."
Child: (looking at the tablet and pointing to it)

Parent: "Oh, sure, the men shouted and down with a lurch, went Horton the Elephant, still on his perch. Tied down to a board that could just scarcely hold him, bump! Horton landed, and then the men sold him. They sold him to the circus. Sold to a circus, then week after week, they showed him to people at 10 cents a peek. They took him to Boston. That's here..."
Child: (pointing at the screen, looking attentively)

Parent: “Poor Horton grew sadder and falter he wouldn't. He said in a hot noisy tent and 'I meant what I said and I said what I meant, an elephant's faithful one hundred percent.' That's weird. Where there is nothing, get out of that."
Child: (continues to point at the screen, looking interested)
Parent: "Then one day the circus now happened to reach a town way down south. Ah! Then what happened? They go to where the bird was. Maybe. Do you think so?"
Child: (nodding slightly, still pointing at the screen)

Parent: “A town way down south, not so far from Palm Beach. That is the bird, where bird go. And drawing a long way up high in the sky, who of all people, should chance to fly by? But, that old good-for-nothing bird, runaway Mayzie, still on vacation, and still just as lazy."
Child: (looking intently at the screen, pointing with more enthusiasm)

Parent: “And spying the flags and the tents just below, she said, ‘Oh, what fun! Why, I'll go to the show!’ And she swooped from the clouds through an open tent door. ‘Good grief,’ gasped the Mayzie. ‘I've seen you before.’ Poor Horton looked up with his face white as chalk. He started to speak, but before he could talk..."
Child: (pointing at the tablet, looking engaged)

Parent: "What has happened? There, rang out of the noisiest ear-splitting squeak from the egg that he'd sat on for 51 weeks. Yes, 51 weeks. What has happened? A thumping, a bumping, a wild live scratching. 'My egg!' Shouted Horton. 'My egg, what? It's hatching!' Let's see what has happened."
Child: (still pointing at the tablet, looking curious)

Parent: ""But it's mine," screamed the bird when she heard the egg crack. The work was all done, now she wanted it back. Which one do you like better? This one? She didn't hatch at all. She just away, play around, and elephant does all the job."
Child: (sitting back, looking at the tablet, thinking)

Parent: ""It's my egg", she shouted, "You stole it from me." Is that true? Elephant didn't steal, right? She asked her... asked him to do that, and then also she promised she will come back soon, but did she come back soon? No, she stayed outside, and she played around. She didn't take care of the bird, the egg. It's elephant who took care of the egg."
Child: (listening, looking a bit confused)
Parent: ""Get off of my nest, and get out of my tree." Poor Horton backed down with a sad, heavy heart. What do you think is in there? Is that a bird? Uh-oh! Bleah! What?"
Child: (looking at the tablet, seemingly focused)

Parent: "At that very instant, the egg burst apart, and out of the pieces of red and white shell, from the egg that he had sat on so long, and so well, Horton the Elephant saw something whizz. It has ears and a tail and a trunk just like his. Is that funny?"
Child: (continues to look at the tablet)
Child: (still focused on the tablet)

Parent: "And the people came, shouting, "What's all this about?" They looked and they stared with their eyes popping out. Then they cheered, and they cheered, and they cheered more and more. They had never seen anything like it before. "My goodness, my gracious." They shouted, "My word! It's something brand new. It is an elephant bird." And it should be and should be a show just like that, because Horton was faithful. He sat and he sat. He knew what he said and he said what he meant. Mm-hmm (affirmative). And they sent him home, happy one hundred percent. That's it. Do you like it?"
